newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU leaders set to put EMU back on course.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders set to put EMU back on course.

text.p: After an early bout of jitters over France's stance on tough borrowing limits for those joining monetary union, Europe's single currency appears to be back on track as EU leaders prepare to meet in Amsterdam next week.

A flurry of diplomatic activity over the past few days has allayed fears that the new French government might scuttle the single currency's timetable by reopening talks on the budget stability pact, a measure designed to keep spending under control among euro participants.

Instead, the Socialist government, committed to pointing Europe in a new direction, seems content to have its focus on employment addressed through two political declarations that will accompany the budget accord.

EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy on Friday said the additions to the pact would be "a sort of economic pillar at the heart of economic and monetary union to allow member states to conduct economic policy in a much more coordinated, close and concerted way."

One resolution will focus on jobs creation while the other will address economic policy coordination among EMU members. Both are seen amplifying what is already included in the Maastricht Treaty and given their non-binding nature should be easily approved.

In addition, the Amsterdam summit will agree on a separate employment chapter, a revision to the treaty long desired by a number of countries but resisted by Germany because of the potential for expensive jobs programmes.
Early drafts of the amendment, however, make no mention of additional spending plans and refer instead to the need for greater EU coordination and cooperation in promoting jobs.

Importantly, the concessions to France on employment should allow EU leaders to ratify the stability and growth pact and re-inject much needed political momentum to economic and monetary union, a project many expect will include a large number of members.

Avinash Persuad, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan in London, says financial markets have concluded a "softened path" for EMU, the consequence of which will be downward pressure on the German mark.
Evidence of such thinking has been seen in recent days with the mark shedding some of the gains made against the dollar and other European currencies earlier in the week.

Whether the soft euro scenario will extend as far as Rome is still unclear, but speaking on German television, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday said he was not opposed to Italy joining EMU.
"Every country has the same chance (to join EMU)," he said. "Italy has the same chance as every other country."

Germany, long committed to a strict interpretation to the entry critiera for the euro, is under pressure to adopt a more flexible posture given the troubles it is having in reining in public expenditure.

Countries wishing to qualify for the euro must bring their public deficits down to three percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1997 and demonstrate that the level of public debt is declining at a satisfactory pace.
German finance minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday he was not keen to engage in a debate over how much latitude governments would have in meeting the Maastricht deficit target.
"I will not engage in a discussion about decimal points," Waigel told German television. "If Germany were to discuss figures like 3.3 or 3.2 percent, others would start to talk about 3.8 percent."

Yet Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, who takes over as president of the European Monetary Institute in July, said in a newspaper interview that a deficit of 3.2 percent would not be a disaster for those wanting to join the euro.
